faqs.a: For US mortgages, the classic comfort zone is 28% front-end / 36% back-end; qualified mortgages cap back-end at 43%. Personal loan and card lenders are looser but still flag anything above 40%. In India, banks typically want total EMIs under 40–50% of net income.

Front-end counts only housing costs (rent or EMI plus tax and insurance) against income. Back-end counts every recurring debt. A renter with no other debt can have 25% front-end and 25% back-end; a homeowner with car and card debt might be 25% front-end but 40% back-end.
faqs.q: Front-end vs back-end DTI — what's the difference?

faqs.a: Three levers: raise income, cut debts, or both. Fastest wins: pay off a small debt entirely (its whole payment disappears from the ratio), refinance to a lower rate, or add income. Avoid the fake fix — extending terms lowers payments but raises total cost.
faqs.q: How can I lower my DTI fast?

faqs.a: No. Lenders count only debt obligations: EMIs, minimum card payments, student loans, alimony, and similar fixed debts. Living expenses matter for your budget but not for the DTI formula — which is exactly why a 'good' DTI can still feel tight.
faqs.q: Does DTI include groceries and subscriptions?

faqs.a: Because DTI uses gross income and ignores your actual cost of living. Expensive cities, childcare, and medical costs can leave nothing despite a 30% DTI. Run the numbers on take-home pay minus all real expenses — that is your true budget.
faqs.q: My DTI is fine but I'm still struggling. Why?

faqs.a: If your back-end DTI is above 36%, usually yes — paying off even one small debt can drop the ratio several points and unlock better rates. But don't drain your emergency fund to do it; lenders also like seeing cash reserves.
faqs.q: Should I pay down debt before applying for a loan?

debt-to-income-ratio-calculator.formula:
Back-end DTI = (housing + car + cards + student + other) / gross monthly income x 100.
Front-end ratio = housing / gross monthly income x 100.
Example: 27,000 / 90,000 x 100 = 30% back-end; 15,000 / 90,000 x 100 = 16.7% front-end.
howTo: Itemize each monthly debt: housing, car, cards, student loans, other.

keyFacts: DTI = all monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income × 100.
Back-end DTI counts every debt; front-end counts housing costs only.
The classic lender rule: 28% front-end / 36% back-end for a comfortable mortgage.

DTI ignores credit score and savings — lenders weigh all three together.

debt-to-income-ratio-calculator.quickAnswer: With ₹90,000 monthly income and ₹27,000 in total debt payments (₹15,000 housing + ₹6,000 car + ₹4,000 cards + ₹2,000 other), your back-end DTI is 30% and your front-end (housing) ratio is 16.7% — a moderate, mortgage-friendly profile. Lenders start worrying above 36% back-end and 28% front-end.

debt-to-income-ratio-calculator.workedExample:
Income ₹90,000/month; housing ₹15,000; car ₹6,000; cards ₹4,000; other ₹2,000:
1. Total debts = 15,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 + 2,000 = ₹27,000.
2. Back-end DTI = 27,000 / 90,000 x 100 = 30%.
3. Front-end = 15,000 / 90,000 x 100 = 16.67%.
4. Verdict: moderate (20–35%) — borrowable, but pay down cards before adding new debt.
